title: Analog in-memory computing signal-to-noise at scale
bottleneck: Analog crossbars compute by summing tiny currents, but as arrays grow, IR drop along wires, device noise, and ADC quantization noise accumulate, degrading signal-to-noise ratio faster than array size grows. Partitioning into small tiles restores accuracy but reintroduces the data-movement costs CIM was meant to eliminate. There is a fundamental scaling law working against large analog arrays.
why_it_blocks: This SNR wall caps analog CIM at modest array sizes, forcing tiled architectures whose efficiency converges back toward digital. The promised orders-of-magnitude advantage shrinks as models grow.
current_state: Architectural tricks (differential cells, noise-aware training, hybrid analog-digital) push usable array sizes up incrementally. Large-model analog CIM at digital accuracy remains unproven. Wire resistance grows with array size, so IR drop along bitlines fundamentally limits how large a single analog crossbar can be before accuracy collapses.
